Casi todo Internet entre ciudades y país: Almost all the Internet between cities and countries travels as pulses of light through glass threads thinner than a hair, sometimes across whole oceans. The light does not escape through the sides because, inside the thread, it bounces completely off the wall: this is total internal reflection.

Un hilo de vidrio más fino que un pelo: A glass thread thinner than a hair
mide una fibra óptica de ancho, como un: wide is an optical fibre, like a hair; the light travels along a core of about 8 µm.
Una fibra óptica es un hilo de vidrio (s: An optical fibre is a glass thread (silica) with two parts: a central **core** and, around it, a **cladding**, all coated in plastic. The core is about 8 µm in long-distance fibres, and the cladding 125 µm.\n\nInfrared light from a laser (of ${LAMBDA} nm, which cannot be seen) travels along it, even if the thread bends. Millions of millions of pulses pass through a single fibre each second, and that is why almost all the Internet between cities and countries travels this way. How does the light avoid escaping through the sides?

When light changes medium it bends. This is Snell's law: $n_1 "sin" θ_1 = n_2 "sin" θ_2$. Going from glass ($n_1 = ${f2(N1)}$) to air ($n_2 = 1$) it **moves away from the normal**: a ray arriving with $θ_1 = ${f0(datos.i0)}°$ leaves at $"sin" θ_2 = ${f2(N1)} · "sin" ${f0(datos.i0)}°$, that is $θ_2 = ${f1(datos.r0)}°$.\n\nIn addition a small part of the light is reflected, the faint reflection you see in a window. If the angle keeps increasing, the exit ray gets closer and closer to the surface…
es el ángulo de incidencia a partir del: is the angle of incidence beyond which the light no longer leaves the core (n = ${f2(N1)} versus ${f2(N2)}).
Dentro de la fibra, el núcleo ($n_1 = ${: Inside the fibre, the core ($n_1 = ${f2(N1)}$) is surrounded by a cladding of slightly less dense glass ($n_2 = ${f2(N2)}$). A ray reaching the wall leaves at $"sin" θ_2 = (n_1/n_2) "sin" θ_1$, and as the angle grows $θ_2$ reaches 90°: the ray leaves grazing the wall.\n\nThat happens exactly at the **critical angle**: $"sin" θ_c = n_2/n_1 = ${f2(N2)}/${f2(N1)}$, that is $θ_c = ${f1(thc)}°$. With a larger angle there is no real solution for the refraction: nothing can get out.

Si el rayo llega a la pared con más de $:
If the ray reaches the wall at more than ${f1(thc)}° (that is, almost parallel to the axis), it is reflected **completely** at each bounce: $R = 100 %$ and $T = 0$. It is not a metallic mirror: nothing is absorbed at the wall, and that is why light can make millions of bounces without being used up.

One detail: the wave does not stop dead at the boundary, but slips into the cladding (evanescent wave) to a depth $d = {λ}/{2π √(n_1^2 sin^2 θ − n_2^2)}$, which with $θ = 85°$ is about **${f1((datos.prof85 || 0) / 1000)} µm**. That is why the cladding has to be much thicker than that.

Move the slider: if the angle drops below ${f1(thc)}°, part of the light escapes at each bounce.
Por qué solo entra la luz bien dirigida: Why only well-directed light gets in
da un cono de aceptación de ±${f1(aMax)}: gives an acceptance cone of ±${f1(aMax)}° in air.
Para que la luz quede atrapada tiene que: For the light to be trapped it has to reach the wall at more than ${f1(thc)}°, that is, at less than $90° − θ_c = ${f1(betaMax)}°$ from the axis. On entering at the tip of the fibre the ray bends (air → glass), so there is a maximum entry angle: $"sin" α_"max" = √(n_1^2 − n_2^2) = ${f3(AN)}$, that is $α_"max" = ${f1(aMax)}°$.\n\nThat number, $NA = √(n_1^2 − n_2^2)$, is the **numerical aperture**. Light arriving within the cone travels along the fibre; light arriving more inclined (in the drawing, ${f0(datos.alfa)}°) leaves through the sides after a few bounces and is lost.

El vidrio no es perfectamente transparen: Glass is not perfectly transparent: it absorbs and scatters a little light. At ${LAMBDA} nm long-distance fibre loses only ${f1(ATEN)} dB per kilometre, the best value in the whole spectrum. In decibels the losses add up, $"dB" = 0.2 · L$, and the power that arrives is $P = P_0 · 10^{−0.2 L/10}$.\n\nOver 100 km that is ${f0(datos.dB100)} dB: a hundredth arrives, ${fP(datos.P100)} of ${f0(P0)} mW, which can still be detected. With amplifiers every few tens of kilometres an ocean can be crossed. And light travels through glass at about 200,000 km/s ($c/n$): it takes ${f2(datos.usPorKm)} µs per kilometre.
